newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: TAP seen struggling to find partners.
newsitem.headline: TAP seen struggling to find partners.

text.p: Portuguese state airline TAP-Air Portugal, which could be privatised next year, will struggle to find strategic partners to help it survive in a fiercely competitive industry, analysts said on Thursday.
"Finding strategic investors for any state-controlled European airline is not an easy matter," said Chris Avery, airlines analyst of French merchant bank Paribas in London.

Charles Donald, European airlines analyst of UBS in London, said: "As it is a small airline, TAP's attraction, relative to other European airlines, to potential Asian or American partners will be limited."

TAP's best bet was to build on its appeal as a "niche" carrier, transporting business travellers and tourists to and from Portugal as the leisure and conference industries grew into the next millennium, analysts said.

The Portuguese state airline is likely to post a profit this year for the first time since 1973 and to be privatised in the second half of 1998, Under-Secretary for Finance Fernando Teixeira dos Santos told reporters late on Wednesday.
He said the government could relinquish its majority holding in TAP, depending on future strategic partnerships.

"The intention of the state is to maintain 51 percent of TAP," he said. But he said that after a detailed review of possible strategic partners, "this scenario (sale of more than 51 percent) cannot be ruled out."
Analysts said that potential strategic partners would look closely at TAP's cost structure and productivity in terms of capacity per employee.
"The fact that TAP may make a profit in one year does not necessarily mean that it is strong financially," Donald said.
The Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres has said that TAP must conclude its restructuring plan before forming any strategic alliance with foreign airlines.

In July 1994 the European Commission authorised a capital increase of 180 billion escudos ($1.06 billion) in government aid for TAP in stages as part of a restructuring plan which laid out financial targets to bring it back to profit by 1997.

TAP is now embroiled in a dispute with its pilots who have said that they will not work overtime or during their holiday periods. Union officials have said some flights could be delayed over Easter because of the protest, which began in mid-March.
TAP should try to pin down code-sharing agreements with other airlines, but would face stiff competition from Spanish state airline Iberia, which has more connections in Latin America, analysts said.
"Feed is crucial to global networks," said Avery. "A north European alliance leader would seek feed from southern Europe and would look at TAP, but it would compete with Iberia."

TAP operates medium-haul flights in Europe and serves long-haul destinations, including the former colonies of Brazil, Angola and Mozambique; South Africa, which has a large Portuguese-speaking community; and the Portuguese territory of Macau.
